analysis.one_liner: Bars executives as well as directors from sitting on the boards of competing corporations.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to keep executives off rivals' boards cleared the Judiciary Committee and sat on the Senate calendar for five months, then was shelved by unanimous consent on October 27, 1990, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would update a 1914 antitrust rule: no one could serve as a director or, for the first time, an officer of two large competing corporations, each with more than $10 million in capital and surplus. It raised the outdated $1 million threshold, carved out exemptions for trivially small overlaps, and adjusted the dollar figures for economic growth each year. The version the Judiciary Committee approved also repealed an old rule requiring railroads and other common carriers to competitively bid contracts when the seller shared a director with the carrier.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers in markets where big companies share directors or top officers. Interlocking seats give rivals a legal channel to exchange information and quietly align; banning the overlaps, with carve-outs for trivial ones, pushes companies to compete on price and quality instead. Antitrust enforcers would also get a standard they can actually apply, since the 1914 dollar threshold had long stopped matching the economy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers in markets where rivals share directors

how_it_helps.text: Extends the ban to corporate officers, not just directors, closing the loophole where competing companies shared a top executive instead of a board seat.

Makes a largely unused 1914 rule workable: it raises the covered-company threshold from $1 million to $10 million, exempts overlaps under 1% of either firm's sales or under 4% of both, and indexes all the dollar figures to the economy so they stay current.
Gives companies a grace period of one year, or until the next regularly scheduled board election, to unwind an overlap before anyone is penalized.

analysis.who_pays: Executives who would have to give up a director or officer seat at a competing company, and the corporations that lose the informal information-sharing those seats provided. In the committee version, suppliers to railroads and other common carriers would also have lost the protection of mandatory competitive bidding on contracts over $50,000 when the seller shared a director with the carrier, because the bill repealed that requirement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives with seats at rival companies

drawbacks.text: The bill loosened the existing rule even as it modernized it: the covered-company threshold jumps from $1 million to $10 million, and companies escape the ban if the overlapping business is under 1% of either firm's sales or under 4% of both, so many overlaps technically illegal in 1989 would have become legal.

The committee-reported version repealed the Clayton Act provision requiring common carriers to competitively bid contracts over $50,000 a year when the seller shared a director, manager, or purchasing agent with the carrier, removing a safeguard for suppliers without inside connections.

Critics of stronger antitrust enforcement argue shared directors among minor competitors do little consumer harm and that forcing companies to reshuffle boards adds compliance cost; the bill's own one-year grace period would have delayed any effect further.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a modest, carefully hedged upgrade to an antitrust rule that had sat mostly unused since 1914. The officer ban and inflation indexing would have made interlocking-directorate law enforceable at large companies, but the bill bought that by raising thresholds, adding sales-based exemptions, and repealing the common-carrier competitive-bidding rule — real concessions to business. None of it took effect, because the bill never reached a vote: neither the protections nor the concessions were ever enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar, but on October 27, 1990 the Senate shelved it by unanimous consent — a way to set a bill aside without anyone having to cast a recorded no vote — and the Congress ended before it ever came to the floor.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on May 16, 1989 with five original cosponsors, including two prominent Republicans, Senator Thurmond and Senator Hatch.
The Judiciary Committee held hearings in July 1989, ordered the bill reported favorably in March 1990, and reported it to the Senate on May 14, 1990 with a substitute amendment and a written report.
The bill was placed on the Senate legislative calendar on May 14, 1990, but the Senate never took it up for a vote.

On October 27, 1990, the Senate indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent, removing it from the calendar with no recorded vote, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations that share directors or officers with competitors keep those seats, and the interlocking-directorate rule remains as hard to enforce in practice as it was before. Railroads and other common carriers lost a would-be gain: the committee version's repeal of the no-bid purchasing rule died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big companies keeping shared directors and officers

against.name: The Senate
against.role: Chamber that never voted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Shelved the bill by unanimous consent on October 27, 1990, a step any single senator could have blocked by objecting; no senator moved to bring it to the floor in the five months it sat on the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Democrat and two well-known Republicans introduced it together, and 2 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored alongside 5 of 55 Senate Democrats — but it died without any recorded vote, so there was never a party-line test.

industries.industry: Executives and boards of large competing corporations
industries.note: Directors and officers could no longer hold seats at a rival firm with over $10 million in capital and surplus, ending a channel through which competitors share information and can soften rivalry. The $10 million threshold and the sales-based exemptions limit how far that prohibition would reach.

The committee-reported bill repealed the rule requiring carriers to competitively bid contracts over $50,000 a year when the seller shared a director or agent with the carrier, letting carriers buy from connected companies without bidding. This gain never took effect because the bill died.
